title: Carl and Laura Lentz on Five Years of Public Judgment: ‘You Can’t Not See God Through Our Story’
summary: Five years ago, Laura Lentz had more advice than she wanted. People who had never met her were telling her what to do about her husband, her marriage and her future. “Getting all these opinions and judgments from the outside when no one really knows what’s going on,” she says. “Only the people that are…
summary_zh: 五年前， Laura Lentz得到的建议比她想要的多。从未见过她的人告诉她该怎么处理她的丈夫，她的婚姻和她的未来。她说： “在没有人真正知道发生了什么的情况下，从外部获得所有这些意见和判断。” “只有那些……
title_zh: 卡尔和劳拉·伦茨谈论五年的公开判断： “你不能从我们的故事中看不到上帝”
content: Five years ago, Laura Lentz had more advice than she wanted. People who had never met her were telling her what to do about her husband, her marriage and her future. “Getting all these opinions and judgments from the outside when no one really knows what’s going on,” she says. “Only the people that are in this know what it takes.” In November 2020, Hillsong founder Brian Houston told staff that Carl Lentz was out at the church’s Manhattan campus, citing breaches of trust. An extramarital affair had come to light. Laura, who had done nothing to land in that spotlight, found herself in it anyway. This month the two of them released a book, Overcoming Infidelity: 10 Conversations To Help Heal the Hurt , and the couple sat down with us to talk about how they got from there to here. “I struggled with a lot of anxiety and just struggling with the opinions of others,” Laura says. “I had to really make sure that didn’t get in here and just remind myself that this is what matters and only we know what’s going on. Lots of therapy has been great. And Jesus, of course, helping through this.” The criticism hasn’t ended, but she says it has changed. “Now I find that’s really gotten quite silent. I think the fruit of our relationship and the fruit of our kids’ lives and where we are now and even writing the book, like you can’t not see God through our story. You can’t not see the miracle through our story.” She is clear about what the book is not. “We’re not out here promoting the book like we’re out to save marriages,” she says. “It’s about me healing, him healing and seeing where that takes us.” The Secrets That Started Small Asked what signs a young married couple should watch for, both of them go to the same place: secrets. “It’s not just big secrets, it’s like the little things,” Laura says. “If you can’t be honest or you’re hiding things from your spouse, those are dangerous and they just compound.” She remembers praying in the weeks before everything surfaced. “I don’t know what it is, but God, you’ve got to get this, just get it out.” Carl says the distance did not begin with the affair. “You don’t start keeping secrets about cheating. You start keeping secrets about fear.” He describes deciding what his wife could handle and keeping the pressure to himself. “It’s when I made the decisions for her on what she was capable of holding,” he says. “Then you stack them and you stack them. By the time you get to the horrific stuff, you’ve already got a pattern of hiding stuff.” What he tells young men now is blunt: get used to being vulnerable with your wife. “It turns out it’s very attractive.” He also rejects the idea that pastors have nobody to tell. “If anybody ever says ‘I didn’t have anybody to be open with,’ I lovingly say I don’t believe you. You chose to not tell anybody.” He says that if he had called Houston on a bad day, he would have been flown out to help. “I did not call. I was not honest. That’s on me.” What Staying Actually Looked Like People tell the spouse who stays that she is brave. Laura is not sure that’s the right word. “It’s so hard to stay, it’s so hard to go,” she says. “Yes, I was brave, I guess, but I was also taking a risk.” She says she would never tell someone to stay in an adulterous relationship, and that she herself saw evidence of change before she did. “There’s gotta be evidence of things that are changing for you to stay and he’s gotta be doing his work.” She describes the early days in small units of time. “We literally went one day at a time. I would wake up and go, okay, I can do today. And that was it.” Carl, a basketball fan, says she has learned the language for it. “Every day, I’m on a one-day contract. That’s an upgrade from a two-hour contract that I was on for quite a long time.” The marriage that came out of that, Laura says, is not the one they had before. “Marriage 2.0 is like so much deeper. Our marriage was fine, but it wasn’t like it is now.” Carl is careful to say it isn’t easy. Some da

title: Meet Elle Limebear, the British Artist Who Turned a School-Assembly Hymn Into a UK No. 1
summary: The daughter of Delirious? frontman Martin Smith rebuilt “Oil in My Lamp” for a new generation, and “Give Me Joy” has spent nine weeks atop the UK Christian chart.
summary_zh: Delirious主唱马丁·史密斯（ Martin Smith ）的女儿为新一代重建了“Oil in My Lamp” ， “Give Me Joy”在英国基督教排行榜上排名第九。
title_zh: 认识英国艺术家Elle Limebear ，他将学校集会赞美诗变成了英国第一
content: Elle Limebear used to have a hard time describing her dad’s job. When classmates asked what he did, she’d say he was in a band, then that it was Christian music, then that it was sort of rocky, and then she’d watch the conversation go nowhere. Some days she wished he were “just a plumber dad.” Her father is Martin Smith, the frontman of Delirious?, the British band behind “History Maker” and “Did You Feel the Mountains Tremble?” and one of the defining worship bands of the late ‘90s and 2000s. She remembers touring the US as a kid, on big tour buses, with people lining up for photos with him. Back home in their English village, “no one really cared.” Limebear now lives in Brighton with her husband, Tom, and their three young children, and the song she’s best known for is one almost every British adult has sung. “Give Me Joy,” released in July, reworks the hymn “Oil in My Lamp.” It debuted at No. 1 on the Official UK Christian & Gospel Singles Chart and has held the top spot for nine weeks since. Decca Records, which announced her signing the same month, calls her its first contemporary Christian artist. The hymn was a fixture of British school assemblies, whether or not the school was religious. “If you sing ‘Oil in My Lamp,’ probably everyone will know it,” Limebear told RELEVANT. “It’s in our childhood. It’s in our bones almost.” She started slipping it into her live sets a few years ago. The reaction surprised her. “There was this eruption of, I know this. I remember being a kid singing this,” she said. “People just belted it, absolutely belted it.” Her husband suggested she rewrite it for people who never grew up singing it. Her first reaction was that the song was already a banner. “What a challenge.” She wrote new verses and melodies and kept the heart of it. When her new label asked whether she had anything to lead with, she figured the answer was no. “It’s a British kind of hymn-like thing,” she said. “Not super cool.” Then she played it for the team, a room of people who, in her words, don’t know Jesus. “They absolutely loved it and it brought them alive. They’re like, I remember singing this song.” The song was only a chorus and a verse at that point, and the response is what pushed her to finish it. Limebear never planned to be a songwriter. At 20 she was set on photography, which felt safe. “I could contain it, control it,” she said. Then she felt God tell her, clearly, to do music. “It didn’t feel like my thought.” She says fear kept her from believing she had anything to bring, and she didn’t know how to write songs. “Back then I was definitely hesitantly walking through these doors full of fear. Now I feel like I’m skipping through them.” The version of England she’s skipping through is a different one from the England she grew up in. She was the only Christian in her whole school, she said, and her youth group “saved my life.” Lately she hears from friends and church leaders across the country about people walking into church out of plain curiosity about Jesus. “There’s this thing called the quiet revival that they say is going on,” she said, “where people are just finding him in all sorts of places.” She remembers being the weirdest person in the room for it. Now, she says, people are discovering that “actually, being a Christian isn’t that weird.” Her takeaway for believers is the same one. “I think we should all be more curious, even as Christians,” she said. “Get more curious. Ask more questions.” Asked what’s behind it, she didn’t pretend to know. “I don’t know is the answer.” She pointed to decades of quiet prayer, from older women in church prayer meetings to families praying at home for relatives to come to faith, and added: “God hears every prayer, doesn’t he?” and “nothing’s wasted.” She also described the last few years in the Church as “good, sad, confusing,” with “lots of walls” coming down, and says she senses something being built back up that looks different from before. She says the change show
content_zh: Elle Limebear曾经很难描述她父亲的工作。 当同学们问他做了什么时, 她会说他在一个乐队里, 然后说这是基督教音乐, 然后是有点摇滚, 然后她会看着谈话无所作为。 她希望他“只是一个水管工爸爸”。 她的父亲是马丁·史密斯(Martin Smith),他是Delirious的前锋?),是“历史制造者”和“你感受了山地的风暴吗?” 背后的英国乐队,也是90年代后期和2000年代的决定性的崇拜乐队之一。 她记得小时候在美国巡演, 在大型旅游巴士上, 人们排队与他合影。 回到家乡的英国村落, Limebear现在与她的丈夫汤姆和他们三个年幼的孩子住在布莱顿,她最著名的一首歌是几乎每个英国成年人都有一首歌. “给我欢乐”,7月发行, 它在英国官方"基督教与福音单行道图"第1期首发并连续9周保持了顶尖位置. Decca唱片公司宣布同月签约,称她为"第一位当代基督教艺术家". 赞美诗是英国学校集会的定律,无论学校是否是宗教. “如果你唱出‘Oil in My Lamp', “这是在我们童年时期。 这几乎是在我们的骨头里。 她几年前开始把它滑入她的现场 反应让她吃惊了. “有一次爆发,我知道这一点。 我还记得小时候唱这个, “人们只是把它系上,绝对把它系上。” 她丈夫建议她为从未长大的歌唱者改写. 她的第一个反应是这首歌已经是一面旗帜. “真是挑战。” 她写了新的诗和旋律,并保持了它的心脏. 当她的新标签问她是否有 任何领导,她认为答案是否定的。 “这是英国的一种赞美诗。 “不是超级酷。” 她为球队演奏, “他们绝对喜欢它,它使他们生还。 他们喜欢, 我记得唱这首歌。 这首歌当时只是一首合唱和一首诗作曲,回应是促使她完成的. Limebear从未计划做作曲家. 20岁时她被设定在摄影上 这感觉很安全 她说,“我可以控制它,控制它。” 然后她觉得上帝告诉她,很明显, 做音乐。 “这不像我的想法。” 她表示害怕让她无法相信她有什么要带的东西, “那时我确实犹豫地走进这些充满恐惧的门去。 现在我觉得自己正在跳过它们。 她跳过英国的版本与她成长的英国不同. 她说她是全校唯一的基督徒, 最近她从全国各地的朋友和教会领袖那里听到人们出于对耶稣的纯粹好奇而走入教堂. 她说 , “ 有一种叫静静的复兴的东西, 他们说,“人们正在各种地方找到他。 ” 她记得是房间里最怪的人 现在,她说,人们正在发现,“事实上,作为一个基督徒并不奇怪。 她的信徒们的外出也是一样 她说,“我认为我们都应该更加好奇,即使是基督徒。” “更加好奇。 问出更多问题。” 她并没有假装知道。 “我不知道答案是什么。 她提到了数十年的静静祈祷,从在教堂祈祷会的年长妇女到在家里为亲戚们祈祷的家庭,并补充说:“上帝听到每一个祈祷,不是吗?”和“没有浪费的东西。 ” 她还将教会的过去几年描述为"美好,悲伤,困惑","许多墙壁"倒下,并说她感觉到一些正在被重建起来的东西看起来与以前不同. 她说是换衣服

title: Can You Build Wealth and Still Follow Jesus? Yes, But Define ‘Enough’ First.
summary: The first decent paycheck can come with an unexpected side of guilt. Maybe your salary no longer starts with a 4, or your savings finally hit a number that once sounded rich. The relief is real. So is the question: Am I allowed to want more? For Christians raised to view wealth with suspicion, professional…
summary_zh: 第一份体面的薪水可能伴随着意想不到的罪恶感。也许你的薪水不再以4开头，或者你的积蓄最终达到了一个曾经听起来很丰富的数字。救济是真实的。所以问题是：我是否被允许想要更多？对于成长为怀疑财富的基督徒来说，专业……
title_zh: 你能在积累财富的同时仍然跟随耶稣吗？是的，但首先定义“足够”。
content: The first decent paycheck can come with an unexpected side of guilt. Maybe your salary no longer starts with a 4, or your savings finally hit a number that once sounded rich. The relief is real. So is the question: Am I allowed to want more? For Christians raised to view wealth with suspicion, professional success can feel surprisingly complicated. The paychecks get bigger, but the question of what faithful ambition looks like often goes unanswered. Paige Whitaker thinks the question is worth asking, and that the guilt is pointed at the wrong thing. “I don’t believe wealth and purpose are competing pursuits,” says Whitaker, brand growth and partnerships manager at 316 Financial, a faith-forward bank. “Throughout Scripture, we see faithful people who were blessed with significant resources. The real question is whether we own our money or our money owns us.” Abraham was rich. So were Job, Lydia and Joseph of Arimathea. Scripture doesn’t treat having money and worshiping it as the same thing. Jesus put it plainly: you just can’t serve two. “Wealth becomes dangerous when it becomes our identity, our measure of success, or the thing we rely on most,” Whitaker says. Define “enough” before you get there One practical move: Define enough before your income makes it easy to keep moving the goalposts. “Purpose acts as a guardrail,” Whitaker says. “It helps us define ‘enough’ and reminds us why we’re pursuing financial success in the first place. Without purpose, it’s easy to spend a lifetime chasing bigger numbers while missing what truly matters.” Write it down. A number for the emergency fund. A lifestyle line you won’t cross even when you could. A giving percentage that goes up with your income instead of down. The point is to make the decision once, on purpose, so you’re not renegotiating it with yourself every time a bonus hits. Ask a different set of questions Building wealth with purpose, Whitaker says, starts by changing the questions. Instead of “how do I get more,” ask what the money is for. She points to serving others, providing for family, supporting churches and investing in communities and causes that matter. Run your own money through it. What does your current budget say you care about? If the honest answer is DoorDash and a car payment, that’s data, and now you know what to change. When the increase comes Markeia Johnson leads the Financial Stewardship Committee at 316 Financial, and she gets specific about what to do when the raise actually lands. “When financial increase comes, our response should be guided by prayer and purpose rather than increased spending,” she says. “Additional resources can be used to reduce debt, build savings, invest for the future, support ministry and help those in need.” Notice what’s missing: “upgrade everything.” Lifestyle creep is the quiet way money takes over. Every raise gets absorbed, enough keeps moving, and ten years in you make three times what you did and feel exactly as stretched. “Having the means to make a purchase does not always make it the right decision,” Johnson says. Money as a tool Both return to Matthew 6:33, where Jesus tells His followers to seek God’s kingdom first. “When we seek God’s Kingdom first, money becomes a tool for stewardship rather than a source of security or identity,” Johnson says. “True prosperity is measured not by how much we possess, but by how faithfully we use what God has entrusted to us.” “Money is a tool, not a destination,” Whitaker says. “Wealth is valuable because of what it enables us to do, not because of what it says about us.” Build wealth. Negotiate the raise. Learn how a Roth IRA works. But decide what the money is for before it starts making those decisions for you. “Wealth is a wonderful servant but a terrible master,” Whitaker says. “The goal isn’t simply to build more wealth. The goal is to use what God has entrusted to us to make a meaningful impact.” This article is presented in partnership with 316 Financial, a faith-forward
content_zh: 首个体面的薪水 会有出乎意料的负罪感 也许你的薪水不再从4分开始 或者你的积蓄终于打入了一度听起来很有钱的数字 解脱是实相. 问题是:我是否可以要求更多? 对于被培养成以怀疑来看待财富的基督徒来说,职业上的成功会感到令人惊讶地复杂. 薪水越来越高,但关于什么是忠诚的野心的问题往往得不到答复。 佩奇·惠特克(Paige Whitaker)认为这个问题值得问起,而内疚被指向了错误的东西. “我不相信财富和目的是相互竞争的追求, ”惠特克说, “我们通过《圣经》看到那些获得大量资源的忠实的人们。 真正的问题是,我们是拥有我们的钱还是拥有我们的钱。” 亚伯拉罕很有钱. 约伯,莉迪亚和阿里玛西亚的约瑟夫也是 圣经不把有钱当做同一件事。 耶稣直言不讳地说, Whitaker说,“当Wealth成为我们的身份、衡量成功或我们最依赖的东西时,Wealth变得危险。” 在你到达之前定义“足够” 。 一个实际动作:在收入允许继续移动门柱之前定义足够。 Whitaker说,“目的充当护卫。 “这帮助我们定义`足够', 却忽略了真正重要的东西。 写下来 紧急基金号码 即使可以, 你也不会跨越生活方式界线。 给定的百分率随着收入的上升而不是下降。 关键是要有目的地做一次决定, Whitaker说,从改变问题开始, 而不是“我怎样得到更多”, 她提到为他人服务,提供家庭,支持教会,投资于社区,并造成这一问题。 自己用自己的钱 你的当前预算是怎么说的? 如果诚实的答案是DoorDash和汽车付款,那就是数据,现在你知道该改变什么。 当增加额出现时,Markeia Johnson 领导金融管理委员会 316 Financial, 她得到了具体如何做 当提高额实际落地。 她说,“当资金增加时,我们的反应应以祈祷和目的为指导,而不是增加开支。” “额外资源可用于减少债务、建立储蓄、对未来进行投资、支持部委和帮助需要帮助的人。” 注意所缺少的:“提升一切。” 生活方式的变态是金钱占据的安静方式. 每次加薪都会被吸收, 足够继续移动, 十年里你做出三倍的功劳, 感觉完全一样拉长。 Johnson说,“拥有购买手段并不总是做出正确的决定。” 钱作为工具 两人回到马太福音6: 33 他的追随者首先寻求上帝的王国. “当我们首先寻求上帝的王国时,金钱成为管理的工具,而不是安全或身份的来源。” “真正的繁荣不是以我们拥有多少来衡量的,而是以我们如何忠实地使用真主所委托我们的东西来衡量的。” Whitaker说:“金钱是一种工具,而不是目的地。” “韦尔斯之所以有价值,是因为韦尔斯使我们能够这样做,而不是因为它对我们所说的话。” 建设财富. 谈判加薪。 学着罗斯爱尔兰共和军的工作原理 但是在它开始为你做那些决定之前 先决定这笔钱是用来做什么的 Whitaker说:“韦尔是一个出色的仆人, “目标不仅仅是创造更多的财富。 目的是利用上帝赋予我们的东西来产生有意义的影响。” 本条是与316 Financial合作提出的,后者是信仰前卫。

title: After the Washington Wizards Lost to the Raptors, They Invited Scottie Barnes Into Their Prayer Circle
summary: In the NBA, the postgame TV interview moves fast. The horn sounds, the star of the night gets steered toward the sideline and a reporter is waiting with a microphone before he’s caught his breath. After the Toronto Raptors beat the Washington Wizards 112-102 on Friday, Oct. 23, the microphone was ready. But Scottie Barnes…
summary_zh: 在NBA ，赛后电视采访进行得很快。喇叭声响起，夜晚的星星被引导到边线，一名记者正在用麦克风等待，直到他喘不过气来。多伦多猛龙队在10月23日星期五以112-102击败华盛顿奇才队后，麦克风准备就绪。但Scottie Barnes…
title_zh: 在华盛顿巫师队输给猛龙队之后，他们邀请了斯科蒂·巴恩斯加入他们的祈祷圈
content: In the NBA, the postgame TV interview moves fast. The horn sounds, the star of the night gets steered toward the sideline and a reporter is waiting with a microphone before he’s caught his breath. After the Toronto Raptors beat the Washington Wizards 112-102 on Friday, Oct. 23, the microphone was ready. But Scottie Barnes was walking across midcourt with a Gatorade towel over his head, headed for the Wizards’ postgame prayer circle. A player in the Washington group waved him over. Barnes stepped in among forward Anthony Gill and a handful of Wizards players, and the circle closed around him. Barnes, Toronto’s 25-year-old forward and a former NBA Rookie of the Year, had just finished with 28 points, 14 rebounds and five assists. Toronto’s TV broadcast, meanwhile, was holding for him. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Bleacher Report (@bleacherreport) “He just took off,” one of the Raptors’ broadcasters said as Barnes joined the huddle. “So we’ll wait a minute for him to return.” A few seconds later, the call caught up to the picture: Barnes was “in the huddle there with the Wizards players, sharing a prayer as the Toronto Raptors come away with this victory.” When the circle broke, there were hugs all around, and Barnes started back across the floor with the towel around his neck. “Here comes Scottie,” the broadcast said, sending it down to the sideline. The microphone was still waiting. Gill, in his seventh season with Washington, was one of five finalists for the J. Walter Kennedy Citizenship Award in 2024, which NBA writers give for community service. He has talked publicly about his faith, too. Sharing the stage with Orlando Magic forward Jonathan Isaac at Liberty University’s convocation in 2024 , he told students that people assume an NBA player has “it all figured out.” “They assume that just because you’ve been blessed with a lot of money, life should be easy,” he said. He also said, “I tell myself I need to be more like Jesus. And what was Jesus? The ultimate servant. So, I serve the people around me.”
content_zh: 在NBA,游戏后电视采访动作快. 一名记者拿着麦克风在等待, 在多伦多猛禽于10月23日(星期五)击败华盛顿巫师112-102后,麦克风已经准备好了. 但史考特·巴恩斯正带着加多拉德的毛巾走过中庭, 华盛顿集团的一位球员向他挥手. 巴恩斯在前锋安东尼·吉尔和少数"巫师"球员中出场,圆圈就围住他. 巴恩斯,多伦多25岁的前锋和前NBA年度Rookie,刚刚完成了28分,14回升和5次助攻. 多伦多的电视广播也支持他。 在Bleacher Report(@bleacherreport)分享的Instagram A文章上, 我们等一等他回来。 数秒钟后,这个电话紧紧抓住了画面:巴恩斯“与巫师队的球员们站在那里,在多伦多猛禽队获得这场胜利时分享祷告。” 圆相破裂后,周围都抱了起来,巴恩斯从对面的地上起,脖子被毛巾缠住. Scottie说, 麦克风还在等呢 吉尔在与华盛顿的第七季中,是2024年J. Walter Kennedy Citizenry奖的5名决赛选手之一,NBA作家们为社区服务献出. 他也公开谈论他的信仰。 他在2024年自由大学的集会上与奥兰多魔术前锋乔纳森·艾萨克分享舞台, 生活应该很轻松。 他还说:"我对自己说,我需要更像耶稣. 耶稣是什么? 终相侍从. 因此,我为身边的人服务。”

title_zh: 福雷斯特·弗兰克宣布《耶稣一代》巡回纪录片将于明年上映
content: Forrest Frank has released the first trailer for The Jesus Generation , a documentary about his record-setting Jesus Generation Tour. Lionsgate will distribute the film, which includes appearances by Rick Rubin, Philip Anthony Mitchell and Sadie Robertson, among others. Forrest posted the teaser to YouTube and Instagram, with a sign-up page for updates at forrestfrank.com . A director and release date haven’t been announced yet. The Jesus Generation Tour ran 29 cities from June 1 at the BOK Center in Tulsa, Oklahoma, to a sold-out finale at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas, where more than 35,000 people came. More than 519,000 people attended in two months, which makes it the biggest Christian music tour in history. It also registered outside Christian music. One count named it the biggest arena tour overall. Pollstar ranked the tour No. 5 on its LIVE75 chart in late June, behind Bad Bunny, BTS, Luke Combs and Iron Maiden, who were all playing stadiums. Pollstar said it was the highest chart position of any artist booked primarily in arenas. Early reported shows averaged about 18,000 tickets a night. Hersheypark Stadium in Pennsylvania drew 27,365 people on June 15, and GEODIS Park in Nashville drew 23,667 four days later. Tori Kelly, Cory Asbury and The Figs supported the tour. Demand was there before the first show. Pollstar reported in December that the tour had already passed 470,000 tickets sold. The growth is steep. His first headline run, the 2024 Child of God Tour, drew 48,246 people over 17 shows. The following year, the Child of God Tour Part 2 drew 214,626 fans to 26 shows. This year’s tour more than doubled that attendance. The music behind it has been on a similar run. Child of God II debuted at No. 12 on the Billboard 200 and logged the most weeks at No. 1 on Billboard’s Top Christian Albums chart. “Your Way’s Better” was the No. 1 Hot Christian Song of 2025 and broke into the Hot 100. Forrest has also placed 70 songs on the Hot Christian Songs chart, the most of any artist. Here is the teaser:

title: Why the Doctrine of Conversion Matters for Membership Interviews
summary: It’s difficult to discern whether someone has been converted if you’re hazy on what conversion is.   The post  Why the Doctrine of Conversion Matters for Membership Interviews  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 如果你不知道什么是皈依，就很难辨别某人是否已经皈依。帖子Why the Doctrine of Conversion Matters for Membership Interviews首次出现在9Marks上。
title_zh: 为什么转换原则对会员面试很重要
content: Abstract: David Burnette explains why the doctrine of conversion is so crucial for pastors and churches as they carry out their responsibilities in affirming new members as believers. We must not only understand what conversion is but also be able to apply it to the lives of real people. After giving some basic reminders about membership interviews and identifying things that we are not looking for as evidence of conversion, Burnette provides four questions to help us evaluate whether a prospective member has been converted. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . “I wasn’t living right. I was getting drunk, partying, just doing whatever I wanted. And then it was like God just stopped me in my tracks. I knew something had to change. That’s when I started coming to church, and one Sunday, I felt like the preacher was talking directly to me. Right then I knew I needed to become a Christian, and I got baptized a few weeks later. That was about a year ago, and ever since then I’ve pretty much been coming to church and trying to do what’s right.” That’s how Ben responded when you asked him how he became a Christian. Ben recently moved to your city, and he just completed your church’s four-week New Members Class. Now, as the final step in the process—often called a “membership interview”—you as a pastor must decide whether you will recommend Ben for membership at the next members’ meeting. For the purposes of this article, I’m concerned primarily with the question of whether Ben is converted. I’m assuming he meets your church’s other membership requirements. No doubt you’ve heard similar testimonies, even if the details differ. There’s been some kind of change in the person’s life, and they seem sincere, but it’s not yet clear that this change was rooted in the gospel. So you’ll need to do some more probing. Putting Our Doctrine of Conversion to Work Testimonies like Ben’s remind us why having a biblical doctrine of conversion is so crucial when it comes to the church’s responsibility to affirm new members as believers. After all, it’s difficult to discern whether someone has been converted if you’re hazy on what conversion is . For an explanation of the doctrine of conversion, see Michael Lawrence, Conversion (Crossway, 2017); see also the article by Gregg Allison titled “You Can’t Make I t Happen: The Spirit and the Doctrine of Conversion” in this issue of Church Matters . Testimonies like Ben’s also remind us that we must be able to apply our doctrine of conversion to real-life people in real-life situations. Some prospective members will be new Christians, while others will be less mature in their faith; some will have been converted for years but still have significant blind spots; still others will think they’re Christians when they haven’t truly been converted. And those aren’t the only complicating factors. Some will have a hard time articulating the very truths they profess; others will fail to mention basic aspects of the gospel in their interview; more than a few will be unsure as to how and when they recognized their need for a Savior. All these factors (and more) mean that wisdom and discernment are needed when we are interviewing prospective members. Reminders for Our Approach Before thinking through some practical ways to probe further with testimonies like Ben’s, a few basic reminders may be helpful. Your Knowledge Is Limited Unlike Jesus, we can’t look into a person’s heart, which means our decisions about someone’s spiritual state are never infallible. The very fact that Jesus gave instructions about excommunication indicates that he knew the church would sometimes welcome in those who weren’t truly converted (see Matt. 18:15–18). Even the apostle Paul was wrong about his one-time co-worker Demas. Prior to Demas’s departure, Paul mentions him twice when he refers to his fellow workers in the gospel ministry (Col. 4:14; Ph lm. 24). Ou

title: Unclear Evangelism Leads to Unclear (and False) Conversions
summary: When we appeal to people’s carnal desires, we should not be surprised when our “converts” are more in love with the world than with our Savior.   The post  Unclear Evangelism Leads to Unclear (and False) Conversions  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 当我们呼吁人们的肉体渴望时，当我们的「皈依者」更爱世界而不是我们的救主时，我们不应该感到惊讶。“不明确的传福音导致不明确（和虚假）的转换”一文首先出现在9Marks上。
title_zh: 不明确的传福音会导致不明确（和虚假）的皈依
content: Abstract: John Lee explains how bad evangelistic methods and approaches can lead to false conversions. When we are unclear about the urgency of conversion, the cost of conversion, or the accountability that should accompany conversion, we risk leaving people deceived about their eternal state. Ultimately, our job is simply to proclaim the gospel clearly, trust God to open people’s hearts to the truth, and provide ongoing discipleship to those who respond in repentance and faith. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . Maybe you’re like me and you grew up in a church that did altar calls. My church’s zeal for evangelism was real, and I can still tell you the names of individuals who came to know the Lord through those gospel presentations. But like me, you may also have walked down the aisle to accept Jesus as your Lord and Savior at least five times. The thing is, I believe I was sincere every time I walked the aisle. So why do it over and over again? There was clearly a misunderstanding, despite my church’s good intentions—and my own. The methodology of our ministry affects the fruit of our ministry. Or as Mark Dever has put it, “What you win them with is what you win them to .” Unclear invitations often lead to confused converts. Below I want to consider three different ways this lack of clarity in our evangelism manifests itself and how this can lead to conversions that, in time, prove themselves false. Unclear Urgency I was a disobedient kid. When my mother was particularly exasperated, she’d count down from ten. I had a choice: either obey or dig my heels in and rebel. But as I grew older, I became immune to her shot clock and more accustomed to her threats. My mom’s words fell on deaf ears. Bad evangelism capitalizes on this kind of “countdown” strategy. It puts eternity in the balance based on a singular moment and a one-time decision to follow God—or abandon him forever. And while unbelievers may initially respond positively, their “faith” often doesn’t last. As a result, they may become immune to the gospel because they assume they’ve already tried it. “But,” you might say, “isn’t conversion an urgent matter? Do we not care about people’s eternal destiny?” Absolutely! But we want to place appropriate pressure on their conscience, not just on their choice. Unbelievers need to make a thoughtful decision rather than simply meeting our demands in a singular moment in time. Panic urges them to turn off their critical thinking for the sake of survival. The focus is on an immediate decision rather than the weight of God’s eternal judgment. Unclear Cost At the same time, panicked evangelism is sometimes replaced with what we might call chill evangelism. Chill evangelism attempts to downplay urgency in order to make the decision to follow Jesus more palatable. To take one example, some recent invitations have defined following Jesus as “doing as he did.” The call is to adopt his behavior, particularly his compassion toward the brokenhearted. But following Jesus is about more than adopting a certain kind of spirituality and lifestyle; it’s also about salvation from the judgment of a holy God. Nor is it something you can dabble in; it requires real sacrifice. Jesus says in Matthew 10:38, “Whoever doesn’t take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” As Bonhoeffer famously said, “When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.” Dietrich Bonhoeffer, The Cost of Discipleship (Simon Schuster, 1959), 89. Conversion costs something. Saying yes to Jesus means saying no to sin, to our own passions, and to our former life. The question is: Does our evangelism draw attention to what people must give up? Conversion doesn’t propel us further toward our goals. Rather, it fundamentally reframes our goals in light of God’s kingdom. When we appeal to people’s carnal desires, we should not be surprised when our “converts” are more in love with the world
content_zh: 摘要:约翰·李(John Lee)解释了糟糕的福音传道方法和方法会导致虚假的转换. 当我们不清楚转换的迫切性,转换的成本,或者在转换时应该承担的责任时,我们冒着让人们对其永恒状态被欺骗的风险. 归根结底,我们的工作只是明确宣示福音,相信上帝为人们打开真理的心扉,并为那些悔改和信仰的人不断提供弟子之道. 编辑说明:这篇文章取自9Marks牧师杂志《教会事务》, 或许你跟我一样, 我的教会对福音的热情是真实的,我仍然可以告诉你通过这些福音演讲来了解主的人的名字。 但和我一样,你也许也走过过道 接受耶稣为主和救世主至少五次 问题是,我相信我每次走过道都是真诚的。 那为什么一遍又一遍? 尽管我的教会有良好意图, 我们部的方法影响了我们部的成果。 或者如马克·迪弗所说的那样,“你以什么赢得他们呢? 不明邀请往往导致混淆的转换. 下面我想考虑一下我们福音派中缺乏明确性的三种不同方式,以及这如何能够导致转变,从而及时证明自己是虚假的。 我是一个不服从命令的孩子 我母亲特别兴奋, 我有一个选择:要么服从,要么挖出我的脚跟来反叛. 但随着我长大了,我变得免疫 她的射钟,更习惯她的威胁。 我妈妈的话听不见。 坏的福音派利用这种“倒计时”战略。 它将永恒置于平衡之中,这种平衡基于一个单一的时刻和一次决定,即顺从真主,或永远抛弃他。 并且虽然不信者一开始会做出正面反应, 因为他们认为自己已经试过了。 " 但是, " 你可能说, " 这不是一个紧迫的问题吗? 难道我们不关心人的永恒命运吗? 当然 但我们要给他们的良心施加适当压力,而不仅仅是给他们的选择。 不信者需要作出深思熟虑的决定,而不是在某一时刻满足我们的要求。 恐慌敦促他们为了生存而停止批判性思维. 重点是立即作出决定,而不是上帝永恒判断的分量。 费用不明 与此同时,惊慌的福音派有时被我们可能称之为寒冷的福音派所取而代之. 冷静的福音派试图贬低紧迫性,以便让决定跟随耶稣更加愉快. 举例来说,最近一些邀请书将跟随耶稣定义为“照他做”。 这个呼吁是采取他的行为,特别是他对心碎者的同情. 但跟随耶稣不仅仅是采取某种精神和生活方式;它也涉及从圣神的判断中取出救赎. 它也不是你能够沉浸在其中的东西;它需要真正的牺牲。 耶稣在Matthew 10:38中说,“谁不拿起十字架跟着我,谁就配不上我。” 正如Bonhoeffer所说:“当基督召唤一个人时,他要他来死。” Dietrich Bonhoeffer,The Cost of Discepleship (Simon Schuster, 1959), 89 (英语). 转换成本很高 对耶稣说"是"意味着对罪恶,对我们自己的激情,以及对我们以前的生活说"不". 问题是:我们的福音派是否引起人们注意人们必须放弃什么? 转换不会推动我们进一步实现目标。 相反,它从根本上根据上帝的王国重新确定了我们的目标。 当我们呼吁人们的性欲时,我们不应该感到惊讶,因为我们的“转变”更加热爱世界。

title: What Conversion Looks Like in Messy People (Like Me)
summary: All sinners, regardless of past trauma, messiness of life, socioeconomic background, or educational attainment must be converted the same way—through repentance and faith in Christ alone.    The post  What Conversion Looks Like in Messy People (Like Me)  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 所有罪人，无论过去的创伤、生活的混乱、社会经济背景或教育程度如何，都必须通过悔改和对基督的信心以同样的方式皈依。帖子What Conversion Looks Like in Messy People (Like Me)首次出现在9Marks上。
title_zh: 乱七八糟的人（像我一样）的转化是什么样子
content: Abstract: Mez McConnell points out that the fruit of conversion looks different in everyone’s life, particularly for those who come out of difficult, or “messy,” backgrounds. McConnell illustrates this point by giving two contrasting conversion stories. Then, based on his own background and his ministry among others with difficult backgrounds, he offers five reminders to help pastors minister to such individuals and discern whether they have, in fact, been converted. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . If you’ve been a pastor for a while, it’s likely that you’ve seen some people convert from difficult backgrounds. The Lord saved me from a very difficult past and has given me a ministry to many who come from a similar place. In this piece, I am going to share two conversion stories: one “clean” story and one messy. In God’s kindness to me, I have seen people like John and Jane (who you’re soon to meet) come to saving faith through the witness of my local church. In considering the similarities and differences in John and Jane’s conversions, I pray you grow in boldness, discernment, and patience as you faithfully proclaim the gospel and help people live it out in their own lives. John, a college student who has been attending your Sunday services for some time, asks to speak with you. You meet up and he tells you about his growing conviction over his sin and of his need to repent and place his faith in Christ (those aren’t the terms he uses, but that’s what he means). You feel sure that he is being genuine and so you pray with him and urge him to trust in Christ. Soon after, John tells you that he is now a Christian and so you put him in touch with a mature believer in the church to begin the discipleship process. As the weeks and months progress, you begin to observe a real spiritual hunger in John as he devours the Bible, attends a small group, and comes regularly to a class on Christian doctrine. John begins to pray earnestly in the public meetings, and he volunteers to serve the church body in a number of different ways. So far, so good. John appears to be “soundly converted.” Conversion Doesn’t Always Look the Same Now, let’s change the story to Jane, a single mom of three with an addiction to cannabis and prescription painkillers. What does conversion look like for her? Should we think about “lowering the bar” for people like Jane from so-called “messy” backgrounds? In other words, should we expect less spiritual fruit from Jane than we do from John? And should we expect the spiritual maturation process to be slower, too? Back to Jane and her cannabis and pill addiction. She is in your office talking about feeling convicted of sin and of her desire to put her faith in Jesus for salvation (again, those aren’t the terms she uses, but that’s what she means). As with John, you feel that she is being genuine, and when she tells you a short time later that she’s now trusting in Jesus, you put her in touch with a mature lady in the church to disciple her. However, unlike John, Jane is irregular when it comes to attending Sunday services. Often she turns up late, if she bothers turning up at all. When she does appear, the children are normally loud and fidgety and cause all manner of distractions to those around them. A few members have commented that there is often a strong smell coming off her when she sits near them (later identified as cannabis). When asked about how she is doing spiritually, she becomes very animated about her faith and is proud of the fact that she has drastically cut down her cannabis consumption. The lady who has been discipling Jane reports that she is sporadic in her attendance at Bible study and that she has only been to one small group meeting since professing faith in Christ. You start to have doubts about the genuineness of Jane’s conversion. Things come to a head one evening when a church member calls to inform yo
content_zh: 摘要:Mez McConnell指出,皈依的果实在每个人的生活中都不同,对那些从困难或 " 迷思 " 背景中出来的人来说尤其如此。 McConnell通过给出两个对比的转换故事来说明这一点. 然后,他根据自己的背景以及他的部会和其他有困难背景的人,提出5个提醒,帮助牧师部长向这些人提供帮助,并查明他们是否实际上已经皈依。 编辑说明:这篇文章取自9Marks牧师杂志《教会事务》, 如果你做了一段时间的牧师, 你可能已经看到一些人从困难的背景皈依。 上帝把我从一个非常艰难的过去中拯救出来,并且给了我一个部属给来自类似地方的许多人. 在这部作品中,我将分享两个转换故事:一个是“干净的”故事,一个是混乱的。 我看见约翰和珍(你们很快会见到他们)这样的人, 在考虑约翰和简的皈依过程中的相似之处和差异时,我祈祷你在忠实地宣示福音并帮助人们在自己的生活中生活的同时,以大胆、分辨和耐心地成长。 约翰,一个大学生 他一直在参加你的星期天服务 一段时间,要求与你说话。 他告诉大家,他越来越相信自己的罪过,需要忏悔和信仰基督(这些不是他所用的条件,而是他的意思)。 你确信他是真的 所以你和他一起祈祷 并且敦促他相信基督 不久,约翰告诉你,他现在是基督徒,所以你让他与教会中成熟的信徒联系,开始门徒礼仪过程. 随着数周和数月的进步,你开始在约翰吞噬"圣经"时,观察到一个真正的精神饥饿,参加了一个小团体,并定期来到一个有关基督教教义的班级. 约翰开始在公开会议上真诚祈祷,他自愿以多种不同的方式为教会机构服务. 目前还不错 约翰看来是“貌似被转化了 ” 。 我们改编成Jane的故事, 她的皈依是什么样子? 我们是否应该考虑让Jane这种来自所谓“迷信”背景的人“降低律师资格”? 换句话说,我们是否应该期望简的精神果实比约翰少? 我们是否应期望精神成熟的过程也放慢? 回到简和她大麻和药瘾。 她正在你办公室里谈论被判定有罪的感觉, 以及她希望相信耶稣以救赎的愿望(这又不是她使用的术语, 与约翰一样,你觉得她很真实,当她稍后告诉你她现在信任耶稣时,你让她在教堂里与一位成熟的女士联系,让她成为门徒。 然而,与约翰不同的是,简在参加星期天礼拜时是不规则的. 她经常迟到,如果她烦恼的话。 当她出现时,孩子们通常声音大而虚无,给周围的人带来各种分心。 少数成员评论说,当她坐在他们(后来被确定为大麻)附近时,经常有强烈的气味从她身上冒出. 当被问到她的精神状况时,她变得非常动画化她的信仰,并对她大幅度削减了大麻消费感到骄傲. 这位纪律严明的女士报告说,她偶尔参加《圣经》的学习,自从她表示相信基督以来,她只参加了一次小组会议。 你开始对简的皈依的真实性产生怀疑。 某天晚上,当一个教会成员打电话通知你时,事情就变得头疼了

title: The Reason for Church: A Review
summary: Rescue us from ourselves? No. Jesus died to rescue us from God’s wrath.    The post  The Reason for Church: A Review  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 把我们从自己手中解救出来？不，耶稣死是为了把我们从神的愤怒中拯救出来。帖子The Reason for Church: A Review首先出现在9Marks上。
title_zh: 建立教会的原因：回顾
content: Abstract: Paul Alexander reviews Brad Edwards’s book The Reason for Church , highlighting strengths of the book’s cultural diagnosis while also identifying weaknesses in its prescription for how our current problems should be addressed by the church and the gospel. Edwards emphasizes how sin has affected the way we relate to one another, but he does not adequately address the way our sin affects our relationship with God. Readers will benefit from many of Edwards’s insights, but those who believe that the church’s primary mission is to make disciples through the proclamation of the gospel will find substantive areas of disagreement with his view of the church and its mission. Brad Edwards, The Reason for Church: Why the Body of Christ Still Matters in an Age of Anxiety, Division, and Radical Individualism . Zondervan, 2025. 240 pp. When many of us first read David Wells’s No Place for Truth back in the day, we felt like we did when we saw our first Trans Am. You know who you are—don’t deny it. I know, Christian cultural analysis is more than just “cool” or “awesome.” It’s public theology for evangelism. But shouldn’t it be at least a little thrilling to apply Christian logic to public trends? The world never tires of rephrasing the Serpent’s question, “Did God really say . . .?” Our age now rallies around a therapeutic spirituality, justified by victimhood as a new virtue, expressed through social media, aflame with anti-institutionalism. That leaves the local church looking so . . . 1900s, which implies we need not just a reason for God but a reason for church. The title of Brad Edwards’s book, The Reason for Church , tips us off that Edwards hews more to the apologetics of Tim Keller than to the systematics of David Wells. Edwards is an intellectually sophisticated critic of the meta-modern malaise. Thankfully, he loves Christ and the church more than anything in this world. He pastors The Table, a PCA congregation in Colorado that subscribes to the Westminster Confession of Faith. This book earned Christianity Today’s 2025 Book of the Year for its well-informed cultural analysis, penetrating insights, shrewd applications, and flecks of gospel gold. After reading it, I was not surprised to learn The Reason for Church also earned Edwards The Gospel Coalition First-Time Author Award. Edwards turns phrases like pancakes, but he’s not a show-off. He’s heartfelt, and he’s got personal stories from ministry in his own local church that verify and illustrate his analysis and applications. He writes like he’s done this before. Approach Edwards articulates his social critique of late modernity as Burkean conservatism, focused through the political lens of Yuval Levin and Jonah Goldberg, filtered through the sociological insight of Charles Murray, and lit by the psychological findings of Jonathan Haidt. The “little platoons” of local mediating institutions that put us shoulder to shoulder with people across the political aisle are disappearing (79, 93; think Putnam’s Bowling Alone ). We are fracturing the republic into politically homogeneous ghettos by ZIP code. With no buffer between the individual and the political, everything becomes political, impersonal, ultimate . . . and contentious. Diagnosis Today, individualism hijacks individuality such that self becomes sacrosanct. Boomers built churches on Peter Drucker’s pragmatism, which ended up offering Sunday consumers “a Coldplay concert with a TED talk” (14, 16). The church’s customer-is-king technique only manipulates our Main Character Syndrome, making church a provider of goods and services, and excusing us for treating each other as non-player participants in a reality where self is still the star of the show (47–48). Therapy teaches us to prize intuitional over institutional spiritualities (28–35, channeling Philip Rieff and Carl Trueman), so people retreat from churches that call them to repent, choosing instead safe spaces that affirm them in sin. Social media disintegrates
content_zh: 摘要:保罗·亚历山大评论了布拉德·爱德华兹所著"教会的理由"一书,强调了该书文化诊断的优点,同时也指出了该书如何由教会和福音书解决我们当前问题处方的弱点. Edwards强调罪恶如何影响我们彼此的关系,但他没有充分处理我们的罪恶如何影响我们与上帝的关系。 读者将会从爱德华兹的许多见解中获益,但那些认为教会的首要使命是通过宣示福音来培养门徒的人会发现他对于教会及其使命的看法存在实质性的分歧. 布拉德·爱德华兹 《教会的理由:为什么基督的身体在焦虑、分裂和激进个人主义的时代仍然重要》,Zondervan,2025年。 当我们许多人第一次读到大卫·威尔斯的《真理无所归宿》时, 你知道自己是谁, 我知道,基督教文化分析不仅仅是“酷”或“优美”的。 这是福音派的公共神学。 将基督教逻辑运用到公众潮流中, 世界从未厌倦重写蛇人的问题,“上帝真的说过吗?” 我们这个时代现在围绕着一种治疗性精神, 以受害者为理由, 这让当地教会看起来如此 1900年代,这意味着我们不仅需要上帝的理由,还需要教会的理由. Brad Edwards的书标题是《教会的理由》, 爱德华兹是一位在知识上精密的批评者,对"元-现代"的弊病进行了批判. 谢天谢地,他更爱基督和教会,比世界上任何事物都要多. 他在科罗拉多州的一个常设仲裁法院会众中担任牧师,赞同威斯敏斯特信仰忏悔书。 这本书赢得了基督教今日2025年的"年度之书",因为它有丰富的文化分析、深入的见解、精通的应用以及福音黄金的花纹。 在读完之后,我并不惊讶地得知"教会的理由"也获得了爱德华兹福音联盟的"第一次作者奖". Edwards的口味就像煎饼, 他的内心深处, 他写得像以前一样。 接近爱德华兹阐述他对后期现代主义的社会批评为伯克南保守主义,通过尤瓦尔·莱文和约拿·高德伯格的政治透镜来聚焦,通过查尔斯·默里的社会学见解来过滤,并被乔纳森·海德的心理发现所点燃. 当地调解机构的“小排”让我们与政治道上的人并肩并肩(79,93;认为普特南的保龄球是孤独的 ) 。 根据ZIP代码,我们把共和国分裂成政治上单一的犹太区。 在个人和政治之间没有缓冲,一切都变成政治的,非人性的,终极的.和有争议. 今天的诊断,个性主义劫持了个性,以至于自我变得神圣. Boomers根据彼得·德鲁克的实用主义建造了教堂,最终提供星期天的消费者们“与TED谈话的冷戏音乐会”(14,16)。 教会的顾客-王牌技术只操控了我们的主要性格综合症,使教会成为商品和服务的提供者,并责怪我们在现实中将对方视为非玩家参与者,而现实中自我仍然是节目的主角(47–48). 治疗教导我们把直觉的奖赏给制度性精神(28–35,引导菲利普·里夫和卡尔·特鲁曼),因此人们从号召他们悔改的教堂中退缩,选择了安全的地方来证实他们的罪恶。 社交媒体解体
author: Jeri Choi

title: Aiming for Conversion in Our Preaching
summary: Worse than offending unbelievers is treating them like they are believers. Instead, we must aim to help sinners see their sin and confess their need for Christ. This spiritual clarity is not cruel, but kind.   The post  Aiming for Conversion in Our Preaching  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 比冒犯非信徒更糟糕的是，像对待信徒一样对待他们。相反，我们必须致力于帮助罪人看到他们的罪，并承认他们需要基督。这种精神上的清晰不是残酷的，而是善良的。在我们的讲道中， “瞄准皈依”一文首次出现在9Marks上。
title_zh: 在我们的讲道中瞄准皈依
content: Abstract: Sam Romine argues that although the preaching that takes place in the weekly gathering should primarily be aimed at believers, pastors should also aim at the conversion of unbelievers in their preaching. He points as evidence to to the prophets of the Old Testament as well as the apostle Paul’s comments about the presence of unbelievers in the gathering in 1 Corinthians 14:23–25. Romine closes with three practical exhortations to help pastors put this into practice. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . Some things are just meant to go together. A warm slice of apple pie with vanilla ice cream. Cozying up with a book on a rainy day. Watching fireworks light up the night sky with a grilled hot dog in hand. Preaching exegetically through a passage and calling for the conversion of sinners—well, that may be taking things a bit too far! As I’ve reflected on preaching with other pastors, it seems there’s a common temptation to underplay preaching for conversion while aiming to preach expositionally as though these two are incompatible or only awkwardly related. Why is this? Some are simply trying to guard against sloppy exposition that ignores the point of the text. Others have been scarred by past experiences of manipulative altar calls and forced invitations, so they seek to distance themselves from these methods. On the other hand, the failure to preach for conversion sometimes arises from biblical convictions. Since the church is for the gathering of believers, why should we take time away from them to tell unbelievers how to have their sins forgiven? Biblical Patterns and Grounds for Preaching for Conversion While I wholeheartedly agree that the Sunday sermon should primarily have God’s people in view, there is biblical precedent to aim for conversion in our preaching. Consider two examples: the Old Testament prophets and the apostle Paul. 1. An Observation from the Old Testament Prophets I love the prophets. They consistently leave me in awe of God’s majesty and glory, as God is shown to be holy and sovereign and, at the same time, kind and gracious. In this they provide a masterful example of how to weave in calls for sinners to repent while still speaking words of correction, comfort, and hope to believers. For instance, nearly all the prophets speak of impending judgment for Israel’s sin and promises of God’s future grace. Hosea pleads with Israel “to return to the LORD your God” (Hos. 14:1). In Joel, God urges the people to “return to Me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning” (Joel 2:12). Amos calls for the people to “seek the LORD and live,” (Amos 5:4) and Zechariah similarly adds, “Return to me, says the LORD of hosts, and I will return to you” (Zech. 1:3). Of course, Israel is not like the church in that God’s Old Covenant people comprised both believers and unbelievers. Yet we can learn from the way the prophets addressed not only the faithful among God’s people but also those with uncircumcised hearts. God’s concern for the salvation of sinners is demonstrated by repeated calls for repentance. 2. Paul’s Sunday Gathering Observation In 1 Corinthians, Paul addresses several topics pertaining to when believers “come together as a church” (1 Cor. 11:18). Here he makes an important yet often overlooked observation about these gatherings: we are to expect unbelievers to be present. Paul knows the church is made up of those who are “in Christ” (for example, see 1 Cor. 1:2, 4), yet he makes room for the attendance of non-Christians in the weekly gathering. We see this in at least two ways. First, he speaks of “outsiders or unbelievers” entering the gathering when the “whole church comes together” (1 Cor. 14:23). These unbelievers are clearly distinguished from the church. Second, Paul desires the conversion of such people, and he speaks of how powerful it is when unbelievers see God’s people worshipping
content_zh: 摘要:萨姆·罗明(Sam Romine)认为,虽然每周集会中进行的传道活动应主要针对信徒,牧师在传道中也应以皈依不信者为目标. 他向"旧约"的先知以及使徒保罗(Paul)指出,他们认为,在1 Corinthian 14:23–25的集会中,有不信者。 罗明最后提出了三个实际的劝告来帮助牧师将这一点付诸实践. 编辑说明:这篇文章取自9Marks牧师杂志《教会事务》, 有些东西只是要一起走 有香草冰淇淋的苹果派 与一书相会于一雨天. 看着烟花用烤热狗放出夜空中来. 透过一段路, 要求改造罪人, 我考虑过与其他牧师一起传道, 似乎有一种常见的诱惑, 为什么? 有些人只是想防止无视案文要点的草率言论。 另一些人则被过去操纵祭坛和强迫邀请的经历所伤痕累累,因此他们试图与这些方法保持距离. 另一方面,不宣扬皈依有时源于圣经信仰. 既然教堂是供信士们聚会的,我们为什么要花时间告诉不信道的人们,他们的罪过怎么得到宽恕呢? 传承转换的圣经模式和基础 虽然我衷心同意星期天的布道应该让上帝的子民来观望,但我们的布道却有以皈依为目的的圣经先例。 考虑两个例子:旧约先知和使徒保罗. 1. 《旧约》先知的观察,我爱先知。 他们总是让我敬畏上帝的光荣和荣耀,因为上帝被证明是神圣和主权的,同时也是仁慈和仁慈的。 他们以此为表率,说明怎样在劝告罪人悔罪的同时,仍对信士说出改正、安慰和希望的话。 例如,几乎所有的先知都谈到即将对以色列的罪过做出判决,并许诺真主今后给予恩惠。 霍西恳求以色列“回到耶和华你的神身边”(霍斯14:1)。 在乔尔,真主敦促众人“全心全意地归依我,斋戒、哭泣、哀悼”(约尔2:12)。 阿莫斯呼吁人民“向耶和华求生”(Amos 5:4),撒迦利亚同样补充道,“归顺我,万能的耶和华说,我将归顺你”(Zech 1:3)。 当然,以色列与教会不同,因为上帝的旧约中的人既包括信徒也包括不信者。 然而,我们可以从先知们对待上帝人民中的忠实者以及那些有未受洗心的人的方式中吸取教训。 上帝对拯救罪人的关注,表现在一再呼吁忏悔. 2. 保罗的 " 星期日聚会观察 " 在一科林斯,保罗谈到与信徒 " 作为教堂一起来 " (第11:18节)有关的几个专题。 在这里,他对这些聚会作了重要但常常被忽视的观察:我们期望那些不信的人在场。 保罗知道教堂是由那些"在基督中"的人所组成的(例如,见1 Cor. 1:2,4),然而他却为非基督徒出席周会提供了空间. 我们至少从两个方面看到这一点。 首先,他在“整个教堂合在一起”时(第1章第14:23节)谈到“外来者或不信者”进入集会。 这些不信者与教会明显不同. 第二,保罗希望这种人的皈依,他说,当不信道的人们看见真主的百姓崇拜的时候,这种皈依是多么强大。
author: Jeri Choi

title: Eight Enemies of Pastoral Friendship
summary: Biblical friendship is not a luxury for pastors. It is one of God's ordinary means of sustaining us for long-term ministry.   The post  Eight Enemies of Pastoral Friendship  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 圣经友谊不是牧师的奢侈品。这是神支持我们长期事奉的常用方法之一。帖子“田园友谊的八个敌人”首先出现在9Marks上。
title_zh: 田园友谊的八个敌人
content: Abstract: Dave Kiehn argues for the importance of friendship for pastors while noting eight different “enemies” that can easily get in the way. These enemies, or obstacles, to pastoral friendships include things like pride, busyness, insecurity, and other issues related to the pastor’s heart and habits. Far from being luxuries, friendships are one of the means God uses to sustain pastors in their work. Pastoral ministry is often described as lonely, but, for most, it doesn’t need to be. From the opening pages of Scripture, God declares that it is not good for man to be alone. Throughout redemptive history, the Lord strengthened his servants through faithful companions. Moses had Joshua. David had Jonathan. Paul had Barnabas, Silas, Timothy, Titus, Luke, and many other fellow laborers. Even our Lord surrounded himself with the Twelve and enjoyed a uniquely close friendship with Peter, James, and John. The church has long recognized the necessity of Christian friendship. Few, though, have captured the beauty of it better than J. C. Ryle: A friend is one of the greatest blessings on earth. Tell me not of money—affection is better than gold; sympathy is better than lands. He is the poor man who has no friends. This world is full of sorrow because it is full of sin. It is a dark place. It is a lonely place. It is a disappointing place. The brightest sunbeam in it is a friend. Friendship halves our troubles and doubles our joys. J. C. Ryle, Practical Religion: Being Plain Papers on the Daily Duties, Experience, Dangers, and Privileges of Professing Christians ( Baker Book House , n.d. ) , 336. Many others have echoed Ryle’s celebration of the blessing of friendship. C. S. Lewis famously observed, “Friendship is born at that moment when one person says to another, ‘What! You too? I thought I was the only one.’” C. S. Lewis, The Four Loves (Geoffrey Bles, 1960), 65. Charles Spurgeon added, “Friendship is one of the sweetest joys of life. Many might have failed beneath the bitterness of their trial had they not found a friend.” Charles H. Spurgeon, “ The Friend of God, ” in The Metropolitan Tabernacle Pulpit , vol. 33 (Passmore & Alabaster, 1887), sermon no. 1938. John Owen reminded us that Christ himself calls us his friends, John Owen, Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost (1657). and Tim Keller observed that the entire history of redemption can be viewed as one great act of divine friendship. Timothy Keller, “Friendship” (sermon, Redeemer Presbyterian Church, May 29, 2005), Gospel in Life, https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/friendship-2/ . Yet if friendship is such a gift, why do so many pastors struggle to cultivate deep, lasting relationships? Sometimes it’s because of a lack of opportunity, though this seems rarer. More often, friendship is lost to enemies in our own hearts and habits. There are definitely more, but here are eight such enemies of friendship to be on the lookout for. 1. Pride: “I Don’t Need Anyone” One of the greatest threats to pastoral friendship, as with any kind of friendship, is pride. Pride whispers to us that mature pastors should be self-sufficient. It convinces us that asking for help is weakness and that admitting struggles will diminish our leadership. Scripture tells a different story. “Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (Prov. 16:18). James reminds us that “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6). Peter illustrates this danger vividly. Jesus had told him and the other disciples that they would fall away, yet Peter confidently declared, “Even though they all fall away, I will not” (Mark 14:29). Within hours he denied Christ three times. Pride convinces us we are strong enough to stand alone. Humility invites other brothers to speak into our lives before we stumble and fall. The tallest tree is often the first to break when the storm comes. Likewise, pastors who refuse the shelter of faithful friendships often discover their weakness o
content_zh: 摘要:戴夫·基恩认为友情对牧师很重要,同时指出八个不同的“敌人”很容易妨碍他们。 这些对牧人友谊的敌人或障碍包括骄傲、忙碌、不安全以及与牧师的心和习惯有关的其他问题。 友谊远非奢侈,而是上帝用来维持牧师工作的手段之一. 牧师部常被形容为孤独, 真主从天经的开篇中宣布,人独处是不好的。 在整个红色的先发制人的历史中,主通过忠实的同伴来强化他的仆人. 摩西有约书亚。 大卫有乔纳森。 保罗有巴拿巴斯,西拉斯,蒂莫西,提图斯,卢克等许多同事. 甚至我们的主也包围了自己与"十二人",并与彼得,詹姆斯和约翰有着独特的亲密友谊. 教堂早就认识到基督教友谊的必要性. 不过,很少有人比J. C. J. C. Ryle,《实际宗教:成为关于基督教徒日常职责、经验、危险和特权的平凡论文》(Baker Book House, n.d.),336。 许多人响应雷尔对友谊的祝福。 C. S. Lewis著名地观察到,“友谊诞生于一个人对另一个人说:`什么! 你也一样? 我以为我是唯一一个。 ' C. S. Lewis, The Four Loves(Geoffrey Bles,1960),65。 Charles Spurgeon补充说,“友谊是生命中最甜蜜的快乐之一。 许多人如果没有找到朋友,可能在痛苦的审判之下失败了。” Charles H. Spurgeon, “The Friend of God,”载于《大都会Tabernacle Pulpit》, 第33卷(Passmore & Alabaster, 1887年),布道编号:No. 1938 (英语). 约翰 欧文提醒我们,基督自己称我们为他的朋友"约翰·欧文""与上帝同为圣父,圣子和圣灵"(1657年). 蒂姆·凯勒(Tim Keller)指出,救赎的整个历史可以被看作是神圣友谊的伟大行为. Timothy Keller, “友谊” (Sermon, Redeemer Presbyterian Church, 2005年5月29日), 《生命中的福音》, https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/friendship-2. 然而,如果友谊是一种礼物,那么为什么这么多的牧师要努力培养深刻而持久的关系? 有时是因为缺乏机会, 更经常的是,友谊在我们自己的心和习惯中被敌人所失去. 肯定还有更多,但这里有8个这样的友谊敌人需要注意。 1. 骄傲: " 我不需要任何人 " 与任何一种友谊一样,对牧民友谊的最大威胁之一是骄傲. 骄傲地告诉我们,成熟的牧师应该自给自足。 它使我们相信,寻求帮助是软弱的,承认斗争将削弱我们的领导能力。 圣经讲述了不同的故事. “在毁灭前自豪,在倒地前骄傲自大”(第16:18号序言)。 詹姆斯提醒我们,“真主反对骄傲者,但优待谦卑者”(Jas 4.6)。 彼得生动地说明了这种危险. 耶稣告诉过他和其他门徒,他们会掉下去,然而彼得自信地宣称,“即使他们都掉下去,我也不会”(马克14:29)。 几个小时之内 他三次否认基督 骄傲让我们相信,我们有足够的力量独立。 谦卑地邀请了其他兄弟 在我们跌倒前 来谈谈我们的生活 最高的一棵树往往是暴风雨来袭时最先被打破的. 同样,拒绝为忠诚的友情提供庇护的牧师也常常发现他们的弱点。
author: Jeri Choi

title: Youth Ministry Deconstructed
summary: One way the church can minister to teenagers is by discipling their parents to be mature followers of Jesus.   The post  Youth Ministry Deconstructed  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 教会施助青少年的一种方法是通过教导他们的父母成为耶稣的成熟追随者。“青年事工解构”一文首次出现在9Marks上。
title_zh: 青年事工解构
content: Abstract: Kyle Hoffsmith commends David Odom’s Youth Ministry Deconstructed , a book that helps churches evaluate and “deconstruct” their current youth ministry aims and practices in order to reconstruct their youth ministry in a way that is biblical, sustainable, and contextual. Hoffsmith highlights four main strengths of the book: it integrates youth ministry into the church as a whole; it encourages youth ministries to partner with parents; it encourages churches to evaluate their current practices; and it encourages churches to focus on spiritual growth rather than numbers. David Odom, Youth Ministry Deconstructed: Rethinking Your Ministry to Build Lasting Faith in Students . B&H Academic, 2026. 288 pages. There is much discussion today about what youth ministry should look like in the church. Some argue that teenagers should be fully integrated into the life of the church and treated as adults, which means that youth ministry (as it is typically understood) largely disappears as children get older. On the other hand, some churches believe that students should have their own age-segmented ministry throughout their high school years, where most of what is taught and planned is specifically for them. And there are plenty of positions in between. This isn’t merely a disagreement over church polity, as all churches must decide how best to minister to the teenagers among them. These young people need to be evangelized, taught, and shepherded in a way that helps them grow into mature followers of Christ “in the midst of a crooked and twisted generation” (Phil. 2:15). I would agree with professor, author, and youth ministry veteran David Odom that youth ministry needs a “deconstruction.” Odom uses this term as a play on words, as many today speak of “deconstructing” their faith. He uses it to exhort churches to tear down, or deconstruct, the structures and strategies they have used for decades to minister to teenagers. This deconstruction phase comprises the book’s first six chapters, as Odom offers metrics for evaluating your youth ministry in various areas, including spiritual growth, discipleship, and discipleship environments. Then chapters 7–10 focus on building back up, or reconstructing, your youth ministry in a way that is biblical, sustainable, and contextual. Church leaders will undoubtedly find places where they differ with Odom’s approach or his specific applications in certain areas, yet the issues and questions he raises are worthy of reflection. Rather than summarize each chapter, I want to commend Youth Ministry Deconstructed to church leaders by highlighting four main strengths of the book. 1. Youth Ministry Fits Within the Church as a Whole There has been concern for a while now about how youth ministry has created silos in the church. The most encouraging thing about this book is that Odom wants to integrate youth ministry within the church as a whole. So, for instance, when it comes to a question like, Should teenagers skip the corporate gathering to go to a youth worship service? Odom says, “Don’t allow a youth-only worship gathering to become a substitute for intergenerational corporate worship. Teenagers in the church benefit both young people and the congregation” (126). And when it comes to the question, Why does youth ministry exist? he points to an example of a student ministry that uses the following discipleship strategy: “The process for the student ministry is the same as the church as a whole” (112). This doesn’t mean that there can’t be spaces for students to learn in age-appropriate settings, but it does mean that churches should prioritize having youth in the main gathering. 2. Youth Ministries Should Partner with Parents This book emphasizes that youth ministries should partner with parents rather than simply connect with them. Furthermore, Odom says, “We can’t talk about student spiritual growth without discussing the spiritual health of parents” (56). God gave students their parents before he

title: Finish the Race: Final Steps in the Transition to a Plurality of Elders
summary: It is easy to get lost in wanting to lead out in change just so we can say we did it, or out of concern to our reputation. But our motivation for change should be to bring greater glory to God and greater health to his church.   The post  Finish the Race: Final Steps in the Transition to a Plurality of Elders  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 我们很容易迷失在想要在变革中发挥领导作用，这样我们就可以说我们做到了，或者出于对我们声誉的关注。但我们改变的动机应该是给神带来更大的荣耀，给祂的教会带来更大的健康。“完成比赛：向多元长老过渡的最后步骤”一文首先出现在9Marks上。
title_zh: 完成竞赛：向多元长老过渡的最后步骤
content: Abstract: Zach Kilpatrick encourages pastors who are transitioning to a plurality of elders to finish the process well by addressing some practical questions. Questions concerning how new elders will be identified, how they will be presented to the congregation, and what this will mean for the church’s existing constitution and bylaws—along with a multitude of other practical issues—may feel less important, but, as Kilpatrick reminds us in this third article of a three-part series, they are vital if the congregation is to have confidence in the men who are selected and in the process as a whole. Ultimately, this transition should be aimed at the glory of God and the building up of his people. You finally did it. You talked your wife into letting you turn the basement into a man cave! However, after receiving approval, you still have to do the work. What size TV will you buy? Where will it go? How much furniture will you have? Will you put anything on the wall? Many practical questions remain. Similarly, leading a change from a single-elder polity to a plurality of elders has final steps that are often overlooked. We know we need to educate the body on the biblical model and its practical benefits. We understand the need for discussions and an official vote. But even after all this, we aren’t done yet. Having discussed the evaluation and education phases of this process in previous articles, we will now look at the final step, which is also vital: execution. A Word of Warning: Remember Your First Love In his letter to the church in Ephesus (Rev. 2:1–7), Jesus commends them for their perseverance and discernment. Thomas R. Schreiner, Revelation , in ESV Expository Commentary , v ol. 12 , 570 – 571. They were known for their commitment to sound doctrine and righteous living. Yet they are rebuked because they had abandoned their first love. Schreiner argues that the Ephesians had stopped loving God and others. Sch r einer , Ibid. , 571. These Christians, who were so committed to doing the right thing, had forgotten why they were doing it in the first place. They had orthodoxy and orthopraxy, but they were missing love. Don’t let this be your story. It is easy to get lost in wanting to lead out in change just so we can say we did it, or out of concern to our reputation. But our motivation for change should be to bring greater glory to God and greater health to his church. So don’t lose focus after the vote is taken. See the process through to the end. Finishing Well Check Your Documents One of the first things to do after there is general agreement to move toward a plurality is to consult the church’s governing documents (bylaws, policies, and procedures). You need to determine how to officially adopt the change. Even if all the members are on board and ready, it still has to accord with your governing documents. If your documents do not allow for having a plurality of elders, then you will need to amend or rewrite them. The congregation will then need to vote to accept the amendments or new constitution. As part of this process, you might consider consulting a trusted attorney who has helped like-minded churches deal with these kinds of issues. They might have insights that help prevent you from making a costly mistake. Identify Elder Candidates Once your documents are in order, you will need to identify qualified elder candidates. How this process is handled will have a significant effect on the congregation’s confidence in the transition. One of the most important questions to answer is who will be responsible for nominating the first elders to serve alongside you. The constitution and bylaws of most elder-led congregational churches make the elders responsible for nominating new elders to the congregation. I think this is the best practice. However, since you are the only elder at the time of this change, you will need to decide whether to nominate qualified men yourself or form a one-time committee to help you. Either way, don

title: We Were Waiting to Die: Suffering as a Missionary for the Sake of the Name
summary: I am here to testify that God is with his people in the midst of their suffering. Jesus promised to be with his people to the end of the age (Matt. 28:20), and he is faithful.    The post  We Were Waiting to Die: Suffering as a Missionary for the Sake of the Name  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 我在这里见证，神与祂的子民同在，在他们的痛苦中。耶稣应许要与祂的百姓同在直到世界的末了（太28:20 ） ，祂是信实的。《我们在等待死亡：为圣名而受苦的传教士》一文首次出现在9马可福音上。
title_zh: 我们在等待死亡：作为传教士为名而受苦
content: Abstract: Tyler Markson shares about his own experience of suffering as a missionary in Central Asia, including an occasion on which he and his teammates expected to die after a grenade exploded in their compound. Reflecting on his experience, Markson identifies four biblical realities of suffering to help missionaries and all Christians respond to suffering faithfully and with hope in God’s promises. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters , the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled “ The Pastor and Suffering .” “Death to Christians.” That’s the English translation of the phrase we found printed on a piece of paper and plastered to the large metal gate at the entrance to our Central Asian compound. My missionary teammates and I were returning from sharing a meal with friends down the street when we found this note around dusk. We snatched the paper off the gate and quickly made our way inside the seemingly secure walls of the compound. The death threat was not a total surprise. Over the last two years, I had grown accustomed to the uncertainty of living in an active war zone. Additionally, the preceding few weeks had been particularly volatile, as we had heard whispers from our local friends that we were no longer welcome in our city. We had gone up to the capital city for a week to let things cool down, and then four of us decided to take a two-day trip back to our home to test things out. It was on the second evening of this trip that we received the note on the gate. As we entered the gate and went through the courtyard, we immediately sat down in the living room to talk about next steps. Before we could begin talking, we heard shouting on the street. At the same time, we saw something thrown over the wall and land on the concrete porch mere feet from where the four of us sat, with only a glass window separating us. As soon as the object hit the concrete, I remember a deafening explosion and my entire field of vision was suddenly an orange-tinted color. I remember thinking, “A grenade just exploded. Did that really happen?” Waiting to Die It did happen. The glass shattered. We fell to the floor, crawled on our hands and knees to the bathroom, turned the light off, and sat in silence. We were stunned and unsure of what would happen next. But we all knew that in our country, attacks often started with a grenade and then people would rush in to finish what they started. We crouched defenseless in that bathroom in Central Asia. It’s the first time in my life I genuinely thought I was going to die. I remember many things going through my mind. I thought of my fiancée. I thought of my family back home in the U.S. I also distinctly remember thinking, “I never thought I would die crouched down in a bathroom.” But I also remember thinking, “If this is where the Lord has for me to die, then that’s okay. He’s worth it . ” For the next half hour, we quoted Scripture out loud, prayed, and waited for what we thought was imminent death. In God’s kindness, the attackers never entered our home. Four Biblical Realities of Suffering Well over a decade has passed since these events took place. By God’s grace, I write these words today from another Central Asian country, where I continue to live with my family and serve as a missionary. I have not experienced another incident of acute suffering like the one just described, but that doesn’t mean this last decade has been free from suffering. As I reflect on my own suffering as a missionary for the sake of the Name, I humbly offer four biblical realities of suffering that apply to all missionaries. 1. Suffering Is Normal Scripture is clear that suffering as a Christian is to be expected. “Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial when it comes upon you to test you, as though something strange were happening to you ” (1 Pet. 4:12). It’s easy enough to read these words, yet we often feel surprised when we encounter suffering. Missionaries enter cultures where Jesus

title: Your People Need to Know the “Why” of Shifting to a Plurality of Elders
summary: It seems the reason God gives pastors a job that is too big for one man is that he never intended for one man to do it alone!   The post  Your People Need to Know the “Why” of Shifting to a Plurality of Elders  appeared first on  9Marks .
summary_zh: 看来，神之所以给牧师一份对一个人来说太大的工作，是因为他从来没有打算让一个人独自完成！ Your People Need to Know the “Why” of Shifting to a Plurality of Elders （你的人民需要知道转向多元长老的“原因” ）一文首先出现在9Marks上。
title_zh: 你的人民需要知道转向多元长老的“原因”
content: Abstract : Zach Kilpatrick encourages pastors to help their congregations see the need for a plurality of elders, first from Scripture and then from the various ways it can bless the church and its pastors. Many Christians aren’t aware of the Bible’s teaching about elders, nor do they recognize the strain that pastoral responsibilities can put on the pastor in a senior pastor model. In this second of three articles dealing with transitioning a church from a single-pastor model to a plurality of elders, Kilpatrick helps pastors think through educating their people on this important change. I never understood algebra until I took physics. Algebra was just abstract numbers until physics put those numbers to work. For instance, the quadratic formula helps determine how long a football can stay in the air and whether a receiver running at a certain speed could catch it. Now I’m interested. That’s what most people want—not just abstract theory but practical application. When leading a church through a major change, you should put both on offer. This article is the second in a three-part series on leading a church from a single-pastor polity to a plurality-of-elders model. As in the previous article, I’m using the terms “pastor” and “elder” interchangeably. In the first article , we saw the importance of evaluating your church’s history to help predict hazards you will likely encounter. In this article, we will see the importance of education in the transition process. Help Them See the Need from Scripture On the day of Pentecost, Peter told the gathered crowd to “Repent and be baptized . . .” (Acts 2:38). However, before he gave this command, he preached a sermon full of reasons why they should eagerly do so. In a similar way, we shouldn’t urge a change in polity until we’ve explained why that change needs to be made. Help your church see how a plurality of elders fits better with the teaching and example we find in the New Testament. Once they grasp the Bible’s model, adorn it with practical blessings that will come from adopting it—more on this in a minute. I’m convinced many Christians would be surprised to learn what Scripture actually says about polity. It’s simply too often assumed rather than understood. Therefore, we need to help our members locate the ecclesial prescriptions in their Bibles. Consider Paul’s example and instructions in Acts 20:17–35: elders should teach publicly and privately; teach believers and evangelize unbelievers; proclaim the “whole counsel of God”; know and care for all members of the flock; and protect the church against false teaching. According to Ephesians 4:11–12, elders are among those whom Christ has given to the church to “equip the saints for the work of ministry.” And when Paul tells Timothy the qualifications for being an elder, he says that elders should “manage [their] own household well,” “care for God’s church,” and be “above reproach” (1 Tim. 3:1–7). Given the breadth of these pastoral responsibilities, it’s not surprising that the New Testament repeatedly underlines there being multiple elders for each local church (Acts 14:23; Titus 1:5; Jas. 5:14). Even on a practical level, a plurality of elders appears to be a more sustainable model for pastoral ministry. But if you don’t educate the congregation on these things, many will never see it. Help Them Feel the Need Once members understand the scope and difficulty of a pastor’s calling, they should begin to see that it is too big for one man, and I believe this is by design. It seems the reason God gives pastors a job that is too big for one man is that he never intended for one man to do it alone! Though we want to avoid coming across as complaining about our job, particularly given that many members also have difficult jobs, we can be honest with them about the strain of pastoring alone. I told the congregation I often had to look at two pastoral responsibilities and choose which one to neglect. There were days when I didn’t have tim

title_zh: 马丁·路德是谁？
content: As a doctoral student, Martin Luther finally had access to the university library. Here, for the first time in his life, he held a complete Bible in his hands. The Bible was venerated in the medieval church, and portions of it were read from the lectionary used in worship services. But Bibles had to be copied by hand, so they were very expensive. Many churches did not even own one. And if they did, most people were illiterate, so they could not read it anyway. No wonder the church had drifted from the Word of God. Yes, the medieval church taught that Jesus died for our sins, a salvation applied at baptism. But if you sinned after that, you had to pay. Each sin that you confessed before a priest could be forgiven, as long as you performed some kind of penance. Even forgiven sins, though, required a temporal punishment, if not in this life, then in purgatory. In the meantime, to be saved, a Christian needed to accumulate enough merit through good works and acts of devotion in order to deserve God’s grace and to earn a place in heaven. Young Luther was no rebel. He took the church’s teaching seriously. Church vocations, with their vows of celibacy and other ascetic disciplines, were thought to be more spiritual and more likely to lead to heaven than the worldly lives of the laity. So Luther became a monk, then a priest. Still, he would agonize over his sins. Once he had access to a Bible, he read it voraciously, and a new picture of God, of Christ, and of salvation started to become clear. The University of Wittenberg was one of the new Renaissance schools that stressed going back to the original sources. The medieval universities taught theology through the method known as scholasticism , using authoritative textbooks and rationalistic disputations. But the original source for Christianity is the Bible. And since Renaissance-style, classical education also taught Greek and Hebrew, it became possible to study the Bible in its original languages, whereas previously it had only been available in a Latin translation. When Luther earned his doctorate, the university put him on faculty and gave him the responsibility of teaching the Bible. In preparing a lecture on the book of Romans, Luther struggled to understand this passage: “The righteous shall live by faith” (Rom. 1:17). Suddenly it hit him: We are justified by grace through faith in the atoning work of Jesus Christ! Luther said, “Here I felt that I was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates.” Meanwhile, it became clearer that the medieval church thought otherwise. It was sponsoring a sale, promising to release Christians from purgatory if they would buy a certificate called an indulgence . People had been taught that they would suffer in penitential fire for seven years for every sin they committed, including those that had been forgiven. Christians were expecting to be in purgatory for thousands of years before they could enter heaven. Of course, they gladly bought indulgences. For Luther, not only was this a cynical scam that exploited the poor (an indulgence cost workers about a week’s wages), it was a monstrous violation of God’s saving Word. On October 31, 1517, Luther nailed to the church door a list of Ninety-Five Theses against the sale of indulgences, which he was willing to debate. Someone, using the newly invented printing press, printed hundreds of copies. Someone else translated them from scholarly Latin into popular German, selling thousands. They soon spread through all of Germany. They were then translated into French, Italian, and English. The Ninety-Five Theses, as we would say today, went viral. The Vatican responded with treatises of its own, which Luther answered. The controversy escalated into other issues. Luther said that the Bible gives no support for indulgences. The Vatican replied that they are authorized by the pope. Luther responded that the Bible is a higher authority than the pope. The Vatican asked Luther how pe

title_zh: 谁是上帝？ 39%的英国成年人不确定
content: “Who is God?” This is the most important question we can ask, yet many people in the United Kingdom are unsure of how to answer it. In this year’s State of Theology survey , 39% of UK adults responded “not sure” to the statement, “There is one true God in three persons: God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit.” The doctrine of the Trinity is fundamental to the Christian faith, because what we believe about God shapes our entire lives. This uncertainty extends beyond the Trinity. This year’s survey results reveal that many UK adults are also unsure about other core Christian beliefs: 39% are unsure of whether Jesus is God 46% are unsure if the Holy Spirit is a personal being 33% are unsure if the Bible is literally true These findings reveal a significant need for clear, faithful Bible teaching. Many people simply do not know what Scripture teaches about God and the Christian faith, and new believers need to be firmly grounded in the truth amid a society that has forgotten many of its biblical roots.
